Here’s what’s tripping you up – and how to get Mistral’s Document AI working reliably.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Which Mistral endpoint do you really need?
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Basic OCR  
   •  Endpoint:  POST https://api.mistral.ai/v1/ocr  
   •  Model:     "mistral-ocr-latest"  
   •  Payload:   {model, document:{type:"document_url", document_url:"…"}, …}

   This endpoint is purpose-built for PDFs (and other “document” formats). It kicks back a pages[] array with markdown, bbox info, etc. – perfect if you just want raw text/structure to push into your own parsing / LLM workflow.

B. Document QnA (chat)  
   •  Endpoint:  POST https://api.mistral.ai/v1/chat/completions  
   •  Chat model: "mistral-small-latest", "mistral-medium-latest", etc.  
   •  In the messages[] you embed the PDF using  
        {type:"document_url", document_url:"https://…" | "data:application/pdf;base64,…"}  

   Use this when you want the LLM to read the doc and answer questions for you.

C. Vision models (Pixtral)  
   •  Accept image_url only (PNG/JPG/… – NOT PDF).  
   •  That 422 “Image content must be a URL or data:image/…” error you hit was because you fed a PDF to Pixtral via image_url.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. What should change in your code?
────────────────────────────────────────
Right now `EstimateExtractorAgent.extractFieldsFromMistralOCR()` builds a chat payload with:

    content: [
      { type: 'text', … },
      { type: 'image_url', image_url: 'data:application/pdf;base64,…' }
    ]

…and targets model "pixtral-12b-2409".  
That will always 422.

Fix #1 – use the OCR endpoint:

```ts
const res = await fetch('https://api.mistral.ai/v1/ocr', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.MISTRAL_API_KEY}`,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    model: 'mistral-ocr-latest',
    document: {
      type: 'document_url',
      document_url: `data:application/pdf;base64,${base64Pdf}`,
    },
    include_image_base64: false,   // text output is plenty for field extraction
  }),
});
const { pages } = await res.json();
const fullMarkdown = pages.map(p => p.markdown).join('\n\n');
```

Fix #2 – if you want to skip OCR and go straight to a chat-level question/answer:

```ts
const chat = await fetch('https://api.mistral.ai/v1/chat/completions', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { … },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    model: 'mistral-small-latest',
    messages: [
      {
        role: 'user',
        content: [
          { type: 'text', text: 'Extract XYZ fields …' },
          { type: 'document_url',
            document_url: `data:application/pdf;base64,${base64Pdf}` },
        ],
      },
    ],
    // optional: document_page_limit, image limits, etc.
  }),
});
```

Key differences:
• `type: "document_url"` (not `image_url`)  
• Chat model, not Pixtral  
• Or use dedicated /ocr endpoint if you only want text first

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Do you need to upload first?
────────────────────────────────────────
Uploading is optional. You can either  
   a) hit `files.upload` → `files.getSignedUrl()` and then send that signed URL as the document_url, or  
   b) embed the base64 PDF directly in the document_url (as the docs show).  
The signed-URL route keeps payloads small and avoids hitting the 20-MB JSON body limit on some hosts.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Your next steps
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Rip out the Pixtral call and switch to the `/v1/ocr` flow (simplest).  
2. Parse the markdown pages the endpoint returns – you already have a text-based extraction pipeline, so just feed that text to your existing field-extraction prompts (or let Mistral do it via QnA).  
3. If you later need conversational Q&A, wrap a chat call around the `document_url` as shown above.

That’s it – once you call the right endpoint/type combo, the 422 disappears and you’ll get clean OCR output to drive the rest of your agents.

Here’s what I’m seeing, why the UI “feels empty,” and the fastest ways to verify that the pipeline really finished.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. What the Vercel log actually shows
────────────────────────────────────────
• The last entry you attached –  
  `EstimateExtractorAgent.extractFieldsFromText: Sequential field extraction completed successfully`  
  – is emitted **mid-pipeline** (inside the Estimate extractor).  
• A few dozen lines later the route writes the final steps (“database_save_complete”, “job-completed”).  
  Those entries are folded under the same invocation in Vercel’s log viewer – you need to click the little   ▸ arrow at the far right of the request row to expand them.  
  (Vercel collapses sub-logs after ~50 lines to keep the table skinny.)

So the work probably did finish, you’re just not seeing the rest of the frame.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Quick sanity-check – does the data exist?
────────────────────────────────────────
Run these SQL snippets in Supabase (or the SQL editor in the dashboard):

```sql
-- 1) Was the job marked completed?
select id,status,error_message,processing_time_ms
from jobs
where id = 'ee628591-cbb7-4dce-ac81-c3eeabab3523';

-- 2) Did job_data get inserted?
select *
from job_data
where job_id = 'ee628591-cbb7-4dce-ac81-c3eeabab3523';

-- 3) Any supplement items?
select count(*) as supplement_count
from supplement_items
where job_id = 'ee628591-cbb7-4dce-ac81-c3eeabab3523';
```

• If those rows are present you’re good – the UI simply isn’t pulling them yet (see next section).  
• If `job_data` is missing we need to look for the “DB error saving job_data” log step.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Why the front-end sometimes shows *nothing* for a minute
────────────────────────────────────────
`Results/[id]/page.tsx → getJobData()` waits for:
  a. `jobs.status === 'completed'` **AND**  
  b. at least one row in `job_data`

Only then does it render the `ResultsDisplay`.  
Because Supabase replication on Vercel can lag ~5-10 s, we retry 10× (5 s apart). If replication takes longer, you’ll get an empty page until you refresh.

Two easy mitigations:

1. Raise the retry count / shorten the delay  
   ```ts
   const MAX_RETRIES = 20
   const RETRY_DELAY_MS = 3000
   ```

2. Show a “Results still propagating… try again in a few seconds” banner when the job is completed but `job_data` is still null (instead of a blank screen).

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Next debugging steps
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Expand the invocation in Vercel’s log UI – confirm you see:
   • `database_save_complete`  
   • `job-completed`  
   If those are missing, the function crashed **after** text extraction. The folded log will usually show the stack-trace right below the last line you pasted.

B. If the log shows `DB save error (job_data): …` we’ll fix the column/constraint mismatch.

C. Want inline visibility?   
   We can emit a *summary log* right before we return the HTTP 200:

```ts
logStreamer.logStep(jobId, 'summary', {
  estimateFields: orchestrationOutput?.estimateExtraction?.data,
  roofFields:     orchestrationOutput?.roofReportExtraction?.data,
  supplements:    supplementsForReport.length
});
```
That summary would appear in the live stream long before Supabase replication finishes.

────────────────────────────────────────
Let me know what you find in steps 2 & 4. Once we know whether `job_data` saved successfully (or see the exact DB error) we can patch it or adjust the UI to wait more gracefully.

Found the culprit — and it’s not the front-end.

Why the log window is basically empty on Vercel  
─────────────────────────────────────────────  
1. `logStreamer` keeps everything in **process memory**.  
2. On Vercel every route (`/api/process`, `/api/jobs/[id]/logs`, etc.) runs in a **separate Lambda** (cold start, brand-new memory).  
3. So:  
   • `POST /api/process` builds up a lovely in-memory log array, finishes, returns 200, then its Lambda is frozen.  
   • A second Lambda (spawned for `/api/jobs/[id]/logs`) has an **empty** `logStreamer` instance, so it can only emit the couple of debug lines that route itself writes (the “sse-stream … closing” message).  
   • Locally (or in earlier dev runs) the same Node process served both routes, so you saw the full fire-hose.

That’s why you get one lonely line instead of the 100-line orchestration story.

Two pragmatic ways to get the fire-hose back  
─────────────────────────────────────────────  
A. Persist logs (Supabase-backed)  
   1. Create a `job_logs` table (`id uuid PK, job_id uuid, ts timestamptz, level text, step text, message text, data jsonb`).  
   2. In `logStreamer.addLog()` add:

   ```ts
   // fire-and-forget – don’t block the critical path
   if (process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY) {
     getSupabaseClient(true /*service role*/ )
       .from('job_logs')
       .insert({
         id: newLog.id,
         job_id: jobId,
         ts: newLog.timestamp.toISOString(),
         level: newLog.level,
         step: newLog.step,
         message: newLog.message,
         data: newLog.data ?? null
       })
       .catch(() => {});    // swallow – logging must never fail the job
   }
   ```

   3. Change the SSE route to:

   • On connect: `select * from job_logs where job_id = $1 order by ts asc`.  
   • Then poll (`limit 100 offset lastRowId`) every 1-2 s or use Supabase Realtime if you want push.  

   Result: works on Vercel, survives restarts, you even get log history later.

B. Stream logs in the **same** Lambda  
   1. Turn `/api/process` into an SSE (multipart) response: upload → start processing → `controller.enqueue()` logs as they happen.  
   2. The client would open ONE connection (no separate `/logs`) and print lines as they arrive.  
   Upside: zero DB writes. Downside: you can’t return `multipart/form-data` and SSE from the same request in browsers today, so you’d need a WebSocket or an `/api/process/start`-then-`/ws/logs` dance. Option A is simpler.

Quick proof-of-concept (5-min patch)  
────────────────────────────────────  
If you just want to see logs immediately:

1. Create the table in SQL editor:

```sql
create table job_logs (
  id uuid primary key,
  job_id uuid not null references jobs(id) on delete cascade,
  ts timestamptz default now(),
  level text,
  step text,
  message text,
  data jsonb
);
```

2. Drop the 15-line “insert” snippet into `log-streamer.ts`.

3. Replace the body of `/api/jobs/[id]/logs` with:

```ts
const { data: rows } = await supabase
  .from('job_logs')
  .select('id, ts, level, step, message, data')
  .eq('job_id', jobId)
  .gt('ts', lastTs)      // lastTs you keep in closure
  .order('ts', { ascending: true });
rows.forEach(r => sendLog({...r, timestamp: r.ts}));
```

That’s literally all – the front-end `LogTerminal` doesn’t change.

Once you deploy that, you’ll get the full verbose stream again (even if the Lambda that processed the job is long gone).

Let me know which route you prefer (DB-backed or same-Lambda streaming) and I can wire up the code for you.

Perfect! 🎉 **Code pushed successfully!**

Now you need to create the `job_logs` table in your Supabase SQL editor. Here's the exact SQL to run:

```sql
create table job_logs (
  id uuid primary key,
  job_id uuid not null references jobs(id) on delete cascade,
  ts timestamptz default now(),
  level text,
  step text,
  message text,
  data jsonb
);

-- Add index for efficient querying by job_id and timestamp
create index idx_job_logs_job_id_ts on job_logs(job_id, ts);
```

**What this fixes:**
1. **Root cause**: Vercel runs each API route in separate Lambdas, so the in-memory `logStreamer` was isolated between `/api/process` and `/api/jobs/[id]/logs`.

2. **Solution**: 
   - `LogStreamer.addLog()` now persists every log to the `job_logs` table (fire-and-forget, won't block processing)
   - The SSE route reads from the database instead of memory
   - Logs survive Lambda restarts and provide full visibility

3. **Backward compatibility**: The front-end `LogTerminal` component doesn't change at all.

Once you run that SQL and the deployment finishes, you should see the full fire-hose of logs again! 🔥

The logs will now show:
- Job creation and orchestration start
- Each agent's detailed processing steps  
- AI calls with prompts and responses
- Field extraction progress
- Database saves
- Final completion

Let me know once you've run the SQL and tested it!
